title: PINNs for the Taylor-Green Vortex
text: Velocity magnitude of the Taylor-Green vortex predicted by the PINN

title: PINNs for the Taylor-Green Vortex
text:
Introduction
The idea behind this project is to solve an inverse problem on the Taylor-Green vortex, a classic 2D unsteady flow, and to recover its viscosity from a few measurements by using a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN). My goal was to understand how to inject physics directly into the training of a network, and how to make it work in practice with PyTorch on a GPU.

title: PINNs for the Taylor-Green Vortex
text:
The Taylor-Green Vortex
The Taylor-Green vortex is an array of counter-rotating eddies that slowly fades away because of viscosity. It is one of the rare unsteady Navier-Stokes flows with a known analytical solution, which makes it the perfect playground: I can generate “measurements” and check precisely whether the network gets the physics right.

title: PINNs for the Taylor-Green Vortex
text:
Physics-Informed Neural Networks
A standard neural network learns from data only. A PINN also learns from the equations. The network takes a point in space and time \((x, y, t)\) and predicts the velocity and the pressure there. Then, thanks to automatic differentiation, I compute the derivatives of its output and measure how badly the Navier-Stokes equations are violated. This violation becomes a term of the loss function, so the network is pushed to be consistent with both the data and the physics.
The trick for the inverse problem is simple: the viscosity is declared as a trainable parameter, optimized at the same time as the weights of the network.

title: PINNs for the Taylor-Green Vortex
text:
My Implementation

The Network
A fully-connected network (MLP) with 3 hidden layers of 128 neurons and SiLU activations. SiLU is smooth, which matters a lot here since the equations require second-order derivatives of the output.


The Loss Function
The total loss is built from several physical ingredients:

Physics: residuals of the momentum and continuity equations at 10 000 random collocation points.
Data: mismatch with 3 000 measurements of the flow.
Boundary and initial conditions: two extra terms constraining the domain edges and the state at \(t=0\).
Pressure gauge: the pressure is only defined up to a constant, so I fixed its mean to remove this ambiguity.

I also experimented with a hard-constraint reparametrization, where the output of the network is multiplied by a function that vanishes on the boundaries and at \(t=0\). Boundary and initial conditions are then satisfied by construction instead of being learned.


Training Strategy
Training happens in two phases, a classic recipe for PINNs:

Adam (1000 epochs, decaying learning rate) to explore the loss landscape and get close to a good solution. The collocation points are resampled every 50 epochs to avoid overfitting a fixed set of points.
L-BFGS (second-order method) to polish the solution on a fixed set of points.

Everything runs on my RTX 3060 with PyTorch.


Visualization

Loss curves for each term, to see which constraint dominates the training.
Relative \(L^2\) error over time for \(u\), \(v\) and \(p\) against the analytical solution.
Animated velocity magnitude predicted by the network.





Evolution of each loss term. The dashed line marks the switch from Adam to L-BFGS.





Relative \(L^2\) error of \(u\), \(v\) and \(p\) over time.





Results and Limitations
Starting from a wrong initial guess (\(\nu = 0.025\), the true value being \(0.01\)), the network recovers the viscosity with a relative error below 1%. The total loss drops from about \(10^2\) to \(10^{-5}\), and the L-BFGS phase brings a spectacular gain of three orders of magnitude over Adam alone. The relative \(L^2\) error stays under \(0.15\%\) for the velocity and around \(0.6\%\) for the pressure, which is harder to learn since it is never measured directly.
That said, I want to be honest about the limits of this first version. The hard-constraint reparametrization I used is built on top of the analytical solution, so the recovered viscosity is a strong sanity check of my pipeline rather than a blind test. Next steps would be to build the constraints from the initial condition only, use periodic boundary conditions (the natural setting of this flow), add noise and sparsity to the measurements, and ensure the viscosity stays positive. Then the real challenge: moving on to flows without analytical solution.

title: LBM Wind Tunnel
text: Smoke streamlines of a NACA 0012 wing profil at \(20°\) and \(Re=500\)

title: LBM Wind Tunnel
text:
Introduction
I built a real-time simulation of a wind tunnel featuring a NACA 0012 airfoil using the Lattice Boltzmann Method (LBM) in Godot 4.2. The main goal of this project was to understand how to implement the LBM from scratch and how to parallelize it. Because I wanted a real-time simulation—both for the challenge and for the pedagogical value of seeing the physics instantly, I chose Godot 4.2, which makes handling the graphical interface, compute shaders, and rendering very accessible.

title: LBM Wind Tunnel
text:
The Lattice Boltzmann Method
The LBM is a numerical method used to simulate fluids based on the Boltzmann equation, which links the microscopic and macroscopic behaviors of fluids. It uses uniform grids (lattices) to predict fluid motion through two main steps:
1. Advection: At each lattice cell, fluid particles move to neighboring cells following a discrete set of velocities, acting as a transport equation.
2. Collision: The advected particles then undergo collisions, relaxing toward their local equilibrium state based on a specific collision operator.

title: LBM Wind Tunnel
text:
My Simulation

Boundary Conditions

Inlet: Used the Zou-He velocity boundary condition to generate the incoming airflow. This method effectively determines the unknown distribution functions at the boundary when Dirichlet conditions are required.
Outlet: Applied a zero-gradient (Neumann) boundary condition to allow the fluid to exit smoothly.
Sponge Zones: Placed a small sponge zone at the inlet and a larger one at the outlet to absorb acoustic waves, relaxing the fluid back to the inlet velocity and base density.
Top/Bottom Walls: Implemented a free-slip (mirror) boundary condition. Particles heading for the wall bounce back symmetrically, conserving their tangential momentum so no artificial friction is induced.
Airfoil: Used a standard bounce-back (no-slip) boundary condition. Particles bounce back in the opposite direction, creating friction, which in turn generates drag and lift.



Collision Operator
I initially started with a standard single-relaxation-time (BGK) operator but quickly upgraded to a Two-Relaxation-Time (TRT) operator due to early convergence issues. This switch significantly improved the simulation’s stability.


Parallel Computing
The physics engine uses the standard D2Q9 lattice model and is entirely written in GLSL, running on my RTX 3060. By utilizing compute shaders, I mapped one lattice cell to one GPU thread. I structured the memory using two Structure of Arrays (SoA) buffers of size \(9 \times N\) to store the current and next-step distribution functions. Running on a \(1600 \times 800\) grid with a time sub-stepping of 35 (computing 35 physics steps before rendering the next frame), the simulation achieves a smooth ~105 physical frames per second.


Visualization
I implemented several real-time visualization modes for the domain:

Vertical Velocity: \(U_y\)
Velocity Magnitude: \(|U|\)
Vorticity: \(\nabla \times U\)
Density: \(\rho\)
Smoke Streamlines: Using a semi-Lagrangian advection scheme coupled with the LBM velocity field.
Instability Tracker: The domain turns pink if NaN or Inf values are detected in the buffers.







Air vertical velocity around a NACA 0012 wing profile at \(11^\circ\) and \(Re=500\)







Air velocity magnitude around a NACA 0012 wing profile at \(11^\circ\) and \(Re=500\)









Air vorticity around a NACA 0012 wing profile at \(11^\circ\) and \(Re=500\)







Air density around a NACA 0012 wing profile at \(11^\circ\) and \(Re=500\)







Results and Limitations
Currently, the model runs quite well up to \(Re \approx 1700\). To maintain a stable physical framerate and prevent divergence at higher Reynolds numbers, the simulation speed must be scaled down to keep the lattice velocity strictly within the incompressibility limit (Mach number \(Ma < 0.3\)). The computed physical values, such as the drag and lift coefficients, correlate well with experimental data for angles of attack \(|\alpha| < 20^\circ\). Additionally, the smoke streamlines look visually accurate.
However, the model is strictly limited to \(Re \approx 1700\) and diverges above this threshold. To fix these instabilities, future work would involve switching to a Multiple-Relaxation-Time (MRT) collision operator, expanding the domain size to reduce blockage ratio effects, implementing local grid refinement, and adding a turbulence model. While these additions would definitely improve stability, they would also drastically increase computational costs.
